anchorData: TRAY (Kisumu school lab, 8 substances, labelled A-H): A table salt (sodium chloride), B water (distilled, 50 mL per beaker), C sand (mainly silicon dioxide), D sulphur powder (yellow), E iron filings (grey), F antacid tablet (chewable, calcium carbonate with magnesium hydroxide), G paracetamol tablet (500 mg), H sugar (sucrose). NOTE: the phenomenon text names seven; the eighth is sugar, and all lessons must use 8. Test conditions: 1 level spatula (about 2 g) of each solid in 50 mL water at about 25 C; a tablet is used whole. WATER TEST: A salt dissolves completely, clear colourless solution. C sand sinks, stays visible, water stays clear. D sulphur floats on top, not wetted, stays yellow. E iron filings sink, are pulled out by a magnet, not dissolved. F antacid crumbles into a cloudy white suspension in water; it fizzes when dropped into dilute vinegar or lemon juice (acid). G paracetamol stays mostly intact, crumbles slowly, little dissolves; no fizz in vinegar. H sugar dissolves completely, clear solution. HEAT TEST (small amount in dry test tube over a Bunsen flame, teacher-led, goggles on): A salt crackles, no melting, no colour change. C sand no change. D sulphur melts to a runny yellow-brown liquid at about 115 C, then burns with a blue flame and a sharp choking smell (sulphur dioxide). E iron filings glow orange-red and turn dull blackish. F antacid stays white and crumbles, no melting. G paracetamol melts at about 169 C and browns. H sugar melts at about 186 C, turns brown, then chars black with a caramel smell. MIXTURE SEPARATION: mixture M = 3 g iron filings + 3 g sand + 3 g salt (total 9 g) in water. Steps: magnet removes iron (recovered 2.9 g); filtration removes sand (recovered 2.8 g after drying); evaporating the filtrate recovers salt (2.7 g). Total recovered 2.9 + 2.8 + 2.7 = 8.4 g; loss 9 - 8.4 = 0.6 g (spillage and sticking to equipment). Salt dissolved in water cannot be separated by filtering or a magnet; it needs evaporation. MEDICINE FACTS: antacid neutralises excess stomach acid, relieving heartburn (acid indigestion); paracetamol relieves pain and fever and does not neutralise acid. Adult paracetamol label: 1 to 2 tablets of 500 mg every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 8 tablets (8 x 500 mg = 4000 mg = 4 g) in 24 hours; more can damage the liver. Antacid taken too often can upset the body's salts and cause constipation or diarrhoea; always follow the label or a health worker's advice. Do not give children adult doses.
characters: Mrs Achieng: chemistry teacher at the Kisumu school who sets up the tray. Learners: Otieno, Wanjiru, Amina and Kipchirchir, working in Group 1 (four learners); the class has 8 groups, each with one tray. Kisumu school lab: the setting; Lake Victoria is nearby. KEBS (Kenya Bureau of Standards): its Diamond Mark of quality appears on product labels. Pharmacy and Poisons Board: regulates medicines in Kenya. Local industry examples: Kericho tea, Magadi soda ash, Mumias/Nzoia sugar, Kenya Pipeline and KenGen geothermal energy at Olkaria in the Rift Valley, Kenyan pharmaceutical manufacturers in Nairobi, nyama choma and ugali as everyday food chemistry. Wanjiru is the learner who asks the puzzling question about why the antacid and paracetamol differ. Otieno's family runs a kiosk, used for the label and expiry-date lesson. Do not invent other specific data about these people.
outcome: The substances behave differently because each has its own set of properties (solubility, magnetism, density, melting and burning behaviour, reaction with acid), which come from what it is made of. Salt and sugar dissolve and cannot be filtered out, sand and iron do not dissolve and can be filtered or pulled out with a magnet, and sulphur burns while sand does not. Chemists use such properties to choose, separate and make materials; the antacid works because it reacts with and neutralises acid, paracetamol works on pain and fever by a different action, and both are harmful in excess, so labels, correct dosage and avoiding substance misuse keep people safe.
conventions: Chemistry = the science that studies matter: its composition, properties, changes and uses. Matter = anything that has mass and occupies space; states = solid, liquid, gas. Property = a characteristic used to identify or use a substance; physical properties (appearance, solubility, magnetism, melting point, density) vs chemical properties (burning, reacting with acid). Classification: element (iron, sulphur), compound (salt, water, sugar, calcium carbonate), mixture (sand-iron-salt mixture M; tablets are mixtures of an active ingredient with binders). Sand is treated as mainly silicon dioxide. Always call the substances by letters A-H and these exact names. Use 'dissolves' for salt and sugar, 'does not dissolve' for sand, iron, sulphur. Use 'filtration', 'magnetic separation', 'evaporation' only. Units: g, mL, C, mg. Branches of chemistry (five): organic, inorganic, physical, analytical, biochemistry. Model: the class Driving Question Board (DQB) model has versions: v1 (Lesson 3), v2 (Lesson 6), final (Lesson 10). Drug = a substance that changes how the body works; prescription = a health worker's written instruction for a medicine; dosage = amount and timing; substance abuse = using a substance in a harmful way or amount. Label items: quality mark, expiry date, ingredients/preservatives, nutritional information, caution messages. Respect is the KICD value and PCIs are life skills, health promotion and consumer protection. Use Kenyan examples throughout and teacher safety rules: no tasting, goggles on, heating by teacher or supervised.
